items.title: BuildPattern::Custom unconditionally watches generated shadow.rs and is always dirty
items.body:
## Actual behavior

In `shadow-rs 2.0.0`, `BuildPattern::rerun_if` emits this directive unconditionally, after the pattern-specific `match`:

```rust
println!("cargo:rerun-if-changed={out_dir}/{DEFINE_SHADOW_RS}");
```

For `BuildPattern::Custom`, this means Cargo watches a file that the same build script writes into its own `OUT_DIR`. Cargo creates its freshness timestamp before invoking the script; the generated `shadow.rs` is therefore always newer than that timestamp. The build script is dirty on every no-op `cargo build`, and every dependent crate recompiles.

A minimal user configuration is:

```rust
ShadowBuilder::builder()
    .build_pattern(BuildPattern::Custom {
        if_path_changed: vec![/* explicit source-control paths */],
        if_env_changed: vec![],
    })
    .build()
    .unwrap();
```

The user-selected custom watch list is then overridden by the generated-file watch.

## Expected behavior

`Custom` should emit only the paths/environment variables requested by the caller (plus the required external metadata env vars), and should not add a self-watch in `OUT_DIR`.

The `rerun-if-changed=$OUT_DIR/shadow.rs` directive appears meaningful only for `BuildPattern::Lazy`; it should be guarded by a pattern match so it is not emitted for `Custom` or `RealTime`.

## Impact and local workaround

This caused a no-op build to rebuild a 12-crate downstream graph in our workspace. We pinned `shadow-rs = "=2.0.0"` and locally clamp the generated files mtime to Cargo invocation timestamp after generation. That avoids the continual rebuild but is necessarily a downstream workaround; correcting the emitted directive is the proper fix.

items.title: Upgrade git2 to >= 0.21 to fix RUSTSEC-2026-0183/0184 unsound advisories
items.body:
**shadow-rs 2.0.0 depends on `git2 ^0.20.0`, which resolves to `git2 0.20.4`.** That git2 version carries two *unsound* rustsec advisories, both patched in `git2 >= 0.21.0`:

- [RUSTSEC-2026-0183](https://rustsec.org/advisories/RUSTSEC-2026-0183): Potential undefined behavior when calling `Remote::list()` (null pointer passed to `slice::from_raw_parts()` when the remote advertises no refs).
- [RUSTSEC-2026-0184](https://rustsec.org/advisories/RUSTSEC-2026-0184): Potential undefined behavior with `Signature` created from null pointers on buffer-created `BlameHunk`.

Because shadow-rs pins `git2 ^0.20.0`, downstream consumers cannot upgrade git2 to the patched `0.21` without breaking the dependency resolution — `cargo-audit` keeps reporting these informational warnings on every build.

**Request**: bump the `git2` dependency to `^0.21` (or the latest compatible major), so consumers get the patched version.

I can open a PR if helpful.

items.title: Incorrect `no_std` feature
items.body:
Hello! Thank you for `shadow-rs`; it solves a very specific problem very well.

I've found an issue with the way that `no_std` is supported in `shadow-rs`: The `no_std` feature is non-additive. This is wrong, since features must only ever add functionality - never remove it.

The particular case of the "`no_std` feature" is actually explicitly discouraged by the `cargo` documentation. Per https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/features.html#feature-unification:

> When a dependency is used by multiple packages, Cargo will use the union of all features enabled on that dependency when building it. This helps ensure that only a single copy of the dependency is used. See the [features section](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/resolver.html#features) of the resolver documentation for more details.
> 
> A consequence of this is that features should be additive. That is, enabling a feature should not disable functionality, and it should usually be safe to enable any combination of features.
> 
> **For example, if you want to optionally support [no_std](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/names/preludes.html#the-no_std-attribute) environments, do not use a no_std feature. Instead, use a std feature that enables std.** For example:
> ```rust
> #![no_std]
> 
> #[cfg(feature = "std")]
> extern crate std;
> 
> #[cfg(feature = "std")]
> pub fn function_that_requires_std() {
>     // ...
> }
> ```

# Impact
The consequence here is that one cannot write a `no_std` application w/optional `std`, if that application has a dependency on `shadow-rs`. This is because, to go from `no_std` to `std`, one not only needs to _add_ the `std` feature, but also _remove_ the `no_std` feature. To my knowledge, there's no way to do this, not even as a workaround - but even if there is, it would not be a sensible workaround.

Optional `std` is by far the most common pattern in the `no_std` ecosystem. Therefore, I would argue that this bug makes `shadow-rs` unusable for the majority of the `no_std` ecosystem.

# Proposed Fix
I did a quick `grep` of the source code, and the only affected line seems to be this:

https://github.com/baoyachi/shadow-rs/blob/544adb4738e9ae8c9917f211ca96edc57a0e04b9/src/shadow.rs#L376

This should be corrected to `#[cfg(feature = "std")]`, which should make the `no_std` feature do absolutely nothing, as it should.

**Breakage**: The above is **not** a breaking change. Anybody relying on a `no_std` environment is guaranteed not to have enabled the `std` feature (since in `lib.rs`, `#![cfg_attr(not(feature = "std"), no_std)]` is what creates the `no_std` environment).

This change therefore guarantees that anybody using a `no_std` environment would experience no breakage, while simultaneously fixing the issue.

**Unfortunately**, outright removing the `no_std` feature would be a breaking change requiring a bump to 2.0. Enabling the feature doesn't change anything, but it might incorrectly convince someone that they've disabled `std` when they haven't - so any bug fix must include some kind of communication about this. I would propose ex. a comment in `Cargo.toml`, in release notes, in the README, and in the (adjusted) examples, all explaining not to enable `no_std`, since it does nothing (despite the name), and that it will be removed one day if/when 2.0 is released.

Ideally there might be a way to emit a compile-time deprecation warning if someone enables / keeps that feature enabled anyway, but I'm not certain of how to do that kind of thing.

items.title: Fast no-op compile for release mode?
items.body:
I'm looking at options for embedding source tree metadata into Rust binaries, and `CLAP_LONG_VERSION ` from `shadow-rs` seems to do the job well.

However, the second project I tried it on is https://github.com/cubing/twsearch/ , which is *much* slower in debug mode and therefore requires developing using release mode. Unfortunately:

| Mode | without `shadow-rs` | with `shadow-rs` |
|-|-|-|
| debug (incremental) | 1.37s | 2.15s |
| debug (no-op) | 0.38s | 0.38s |
| release (incremental) | 5.45s | 6.13s |
| release (no-op) | 0.34s | 🚨 6.25s |

We do have some situations where we expect the no-op compilation to be fast, and we can't really handle an extra 6 seconds for that.

Is there a simple way to skip the compilation if the following hold?

- The commit hash is unchanged.
- The build time is within, say… one hour of the previously used time?

Rounding down to the nearest hour would also work, and perhaps avoid implying extra precision for incremental compiles.

items.title: Separate out non-reproducible variables
Building error messages may also require recording
shadow-rs does not report error with git "dubious ownership" fatal error
items.body:
Since CVE-2022-24765, new git version adds an ownership check functionality, and if git owner != current uid, `git` command would report such error:

```
# git status
fatal: detected dubious ownership in repository at '/example'
To add an exception for this directory, call:

	git config --global --add safe.directory /example
```

However, shadow-rs would silently ignore the error, and returns empty values for git-related consts.

Reproduce:

1. Initialize an empty project, with a non-root user and files in "Setup" in shadow-rs README (shadow-rs 0.32.0)
3. Add `println!("{}", build::CLAP_LONG_VERSION);` in `main()`
4. `git init` and `git commit -a`
5. Build with same non-root user:

   ```
   0.1.0
   branch:master
   commit_hash:d423f07a
   build_time:2024-08-21 17:02:35 +08:00
   build_env:rustc 1.80.1 (3f5fd8dd4 2024-08-06),stable-x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
   ```
6. Use `su` to change user to root (Don't use `sudo` as [`git` would try check this with `SUDO_USER` env](https://github.com/git/git/blob/80ccd8a2602820fdf896a8e8894305225f86f61d/git-compat-util.h#L581)). `git status` in root would report this fatal error.
7. `cargo clean` and build with root:

   ```
   0.1.0
   branch:
   commit_hash:
   build_time:2024-08-21 17:05:18 +08:00
   build_env:rustc 1.80.1 (3f5fd8dd4 2024-08-06),stable-x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
   ```

This could make it hard to debug when building Rust projects with Docker (by default it uses root inside container), especially in CI environment (to be frankly this spent me an afternoon to find the bug).

items.title: Consider generating a struct, or otherwise simplify usage
items.body:
TL;DR: make it easier to write shared code interfacing `shadow`'s output.

Currently, `shadow` only generates `pub const VAR: &str` variables - it's great as is, but is also quite a bit unwieldy, leading to a lot of boilerplate in multi-binary projects.

There are two main benefits to this approach:

- easier manipulation and code decoupling - if I want to write display methods, I could have functions accepting a reference to that struct
- API documentation is easier - just look up said structure

This also ties into what @epage wrote in https://github.com/baoyachi/shadow-rs/issues/75#issuecomment-1048035937 - such a struct would work as an accessor. Or rather, structs, as it would be then split per-source (git, rust, etc).

In my project I have a struct (not using all variables), which could easily be made as a part of code generation, like this:

```rust
pub struct BuildInfo {
    pub version_major: &'static str,
    pub version_minor: &'static str,
    pub version_patch: &'static str,
    pub version_pre: &'static str,
    pub git_commit_hash: &'static str,
    pub git_short_hash: &'static str,
    pub git_clean: bool,
    pub build_type: &'static str,
    pub cargo_version: &'static str,
    pub rust_version: &'static str,
    pub rust_channel: &'static str,
    pub target: &'static str,
}
```

which is then initialized with:

```rust
pub(crate) const BUILD_INFO: BuildInfo = BuildInfo {
    version_major: PKG_VERSION_MAJOR,
    version_minor: PKG_VERSION_MINOR,
    version_patch: PKG_VERSION_PATCH,
    version_pre: PKG_VERSION_PRE,
    git_commit_hash: COMMIT_HASH,
    git_short_hash: SHORT_COMMIT,
    git_clean: GIT_CLEAN,
    build_type: BUILD_RUST_CHANNEL,
    cargo_version: CARGO_VERSION,
    rust_version: RUST_VERSION,
    rust_channel: RUST_CHANNEL,
    target: BUILD_TARGET,
};
```
